title: What logic is
description: Logic evaluates arguments, sorting good reasoning from bad; it studies what follows from what. The word comes from Greek logos, 'word, reason'.

facts.text: Logic's central use is evaluating arguments: sorting the good ones from the bad. It can be called the science of what follows from what.
'Logic' comes, through Latin logica, from Greek logike (techne), 'the reasoning art', from logos, meaning 'word' and 'reason'.

title: Critical thinking as reflective thought
description: John Dewey's 1910 'reflective thought', the root of the educational idea of critical thinking: careful consideration of a belief in the light of the grounds that support it.

facts.text: In How We Think (1910), John Dewey defined reflective thought as active, persistent and careful consideration of any belief in the light of the grounds that support it; the educational goal of critical thinking traces back to him.
Dewey wrote in How We Think: 'The essence of critical thinking is suspended judgment.'

title: What an argument is in logic
description: In logic an argument is not a quarrel but a set of claims, some offered as reasons for another. A bare assertion or a story is not an argument.

facts.text: In everyday speech 'argument' can mean a quarrel or shouting match; in logic it means reasons offered in support of a claim. Shouting matches are just disagreements, not arguments in logic's sense.
An argument is a set of statements, some of which (the premises) are offered as reasons for thinking that another (the conclusion) is true.

To tell whether an argument is present, ask whether someone is trying to establish a statement as true by basing it on another statement. If not, there is no argument, and an argument needs at least two separate statements.
Simply asserting a view, however heatedly, is not giving an argument; offering a reason for the view is.

title: Monty Python's Argument Clinic
description: In Monty Python's 1972 'Argument Clinic', a customer pays for an argument and gets contradiction; his protest captures logic's idea of an argument.

facts.text: Monty Python's 'Argument Clinic' sketch, from a 1972 episode of Monty Python's Flying Circus, has a customer pay for an argument and get little but contradiction.

In the sketch, the customer protests that an argument isn't just contradiction but 'a connected series of statements' to establish a proposition; philosophy teachers use it to introduce the logician's sense of argument.

title: Claims: sentences that can be true or false
description: A claim (statement) is a sentence that can be true or false. A false claim is still a claim. Premises and conclusions are always claims.

facts.text: In logic, a statement (or claim) is a sentence that can be true or false, like 'The Nile is a river in northeastern Africa'. A false sentence such as 'The Yangtze is a river in Japan' is still a statement, just a false one.
Premises and conclusions are both statements, so only sentences that can be true or false can serve as either; what matters is that it makes sense to ask whether the sentence is true or false.

title: Questions, commands and exclamations
description: Questions, commands and exclamations are neither true nor false, so they are not claims and cannot be premises or conclusions. Answers to questions are claims.

facts.text: A question such as 'Are you sleepy yet?' is neither true nor false, but an answer such as 'I am not sleepy' is. Questions are not claims; answers are.
Commands such as 'Wake up!' and exclamations such as 'Ouch!' are neither true nor false, so they are not claims.

title: Factual claims
description: A factual (descriptive) claim says what is the case and can be checked by observation or research. A wrong factual claim is still a factual claim.

facts.text: A factual claim can be verified through observation or research: 'Mice are animals' is a fact. Such descriptive statements say what is in fact the case.
A factual claim that turns out to be wrong is still a factual claim, just an erroneous one: sources can confirm or refute it.

title: Opinions of taste
description: Opinions such as 'mice make the best pets' or 'blue is the best color' are held without evidence that could settle them for everyone.

facts.text: An opinion is a statement someone holds to be true without supporting evidence: 'Mice make the best pets' and 'Blue is the best color' are opinions.

title: Value judgments
description: A value judgment (normative claim) says what ought to be, measured against a standard such as a moral or legal one; words like should, ought, good and bad signal it.

facts.text: Normative statements say what ought to be the case, relative to a standard of evaluation such as a moral or legal one; words like should, ought, good and bad often signal them. Descriptive statements say what is the case.

title: Premises and conclusions
description: Premises are the reasons in an argument; the conclusion is the claim they support. 'Premise' means 'set before'; 'conclude' comes from Latin for 'to shut'. Standard form lists premises, then the conclusion.

facts.text: The reasons offered in an argument are called premises; the claim they are offered for is called the conclusion.

'Premise' comes from Medieval Latin praemissa, '(the proposition) set before', from praemittere, 'to send forward, put before'. 'Conclusion' comes from Latin concludere, 'to shut up, enclose', from claudere, 'to shut'.
Putting an argument in standard form means numbering the premises and writing the conclusion last, marked 'therefore' or with the symbol for therefore, three dots.

An argument can state its conclusion first, in the middle or last, as in 'The gardener did it. After all, it was either the butler or the gardener. And the butler didn't do it.' A single sentence can hold a whole argument: 'The butler has an alibi; so they cannot have done it.'

title: Premise and conclusion indicator words
description: Words like so, therefore and thus usually flag a conclusion; because, since and given that usually flag a premise. They are not failsafe: 'since 1999' and 'so happy' signal no argument.

facts.text: Conclusion indicator words include so, therefore, hence, thus, accordingly and consequently.
Premise indicator words include since, because, for, as and given that.
Indicator words don't always work as indicators: in 'I have been running competitively since 1999' and 'I am so happy', since and so signal no argument, so their mere presence doesn't prove one.

title: The unstated premise
description: Many arguments rely on a premise they never state (an enthymeme). Supply the most plausible claim that makes the conclusion follow (the principle of charity); 'should' conclusions often hide a 'should' premise.

facts.text: An argument presented with at least one part left unstated is called an enthymeme; the unstated part is often a suppressed premise.
A missing premise is one an argument needs in order to work but doesn't state explicitly; making missing premises explicit is a central part of reconstructing an argument.
The principle of charity: when reconstructing an argument, make it as strong as possible, supplying the most plausible missing premises that let the conclusion follow.
An argument with a normative conclusion, about what should be, often depends on a normative premise that is not stated explicitly.

title: Explanations versus arguments
description: An argument tries to show that a claim is true; an explanation shows why a claim already accepted is true. Both can use 'because'.

facts.text: An argument tries to establish that its conclusion is true; an explanation tries to establish why something already taken to be true is true.

Explaining aims to increase the audience's understanding; arguing aims to make a standpoint acceptable. An explainer believes the audience already accepts what is being explained; an arguer believes it doesn't yet.
Answering 'Why did this metal expand?' with 'It was heated, and all metals expand when heated' gives explanatory reasons: it helps the questioner understand why, rather than proving that it expanded.

title: Arguments in chains
description: In an extended argument one conclusion becomes the premise of the next. A claim can be an intermediate conclusion; the main conclusion supports nothing further.

facts.text: An extended argument has at least one premise that is itself supported by further reasons; very often arguments have this more complex structure.
An example of a chain: 'I searched the kitchen and didn't find the keys, so they're not in the kitchen. The keys are either in the kitchen or the bedroom, so they're in the bedroom.'
A statement that is supported by a premise and in turn supports the main conclusion is an intermediate conclusion: one and the same statement can be both a premise and a conclusion.
The main conclusion is the statement that depends on others but doesn't itself support any other statement in the argument; a subargument gives indirect support to it.

title: Dewey's subway decision
description: A student's account in Dewey's How We Think (1910): seeing a clock at 12.20, he reasons his way to the subway express to reach a one o'clock engagement.

facts.text: In How We Think (1910), Dewey printed a student's account, taken almost verbatim from class papers: on 16th Street a clock showed 12.20, reminding him of an engagement at 124th Street at one o'clock.

The surface car down had taken an hour, so going back that way would make him about twenty minutes late; he weighed the subway express and the elevated, chose the subway as quicker and nearer his destination, and arrived by one o'clock.

title: Deduction
description: Deduction is reasoning in which the premises are meant to guarantee the conclusion: if they are true, the conclusion must be. A counterexample shows the guarantee fails.

facts.text: A deductive argument is meant to have premises that guarantee its conclusion: if the premises are true, the conclusion must be true.
forall x's argument 'Either the butler or the gardener did it. The butler didn't do it. So the gardener did it.' is one where true premises leave no way for the conclusion to be false.
A counterexample to an argument is a case in which its premises are all true and its conclusion is not; if one exists, the premises don't guarantee the conclusion.
'If the driver did it, the maid didn't. The maid didn't do it. So the driver did it.' has a counterexample: a third person did it, so the premises are true and the conclusion false.
Aristotle recognized two kinds of argument: deduction (sullogismos) and induction (epagoge), which he described as argument from the particular to the universal.

title: Validity
description: An argument is valid when it's impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false. Validity comes from form, not from whether the premises are actually true.

facts.text: An argument is valid if it is impossible for all its premises to be true and its conclusion false; validity does not depend on whether the premises are actually true.
forall x calls 'Oranges are either fruit or musical instruments. Oranges are not fruit. So oranges are musical instruments.' valid: if both premises were true, the conclusion would have to be.
Validity is set by an argument's logical form: every argument of the form 'All A are B; no B are C; so no A are C' is valid, whatever A, B and C are.
'All toasters are items made of gold. All items made of gold are time-travel devices. So all toasters are time-travel devices.' is valid even though its premises are false.
'London is in England. Beijing is in China. So Paris is in France.' has all true sentences but is invalid: the premises could stay true while the conclusion became false.
forall x: 'It is often said that logic doesn't care about feelings. Actually, it doesn't care about facts, either.'

title: Soundness
description: An argument is sound when it is valid and all its premises are actually true, so its conclusion must be true. To rebut one, attack a premise or the form; a flawed argument does not make its conclusion false.

facts.text: An argument is sound if it is valid and all its premises are actually true; a sound argument's conclusion must therefore be true.
To rebut an argument you can show that one or more premises are not true, or that the argument is not valid; logic itself only helps with the second.
Whether an argument's premises are actually true is usually settled by other fields and research, almost never by logic itself.
Invalid arguments, and valid but unsound ones, can still have true conclusions; finding an argument flawed is not, by itself, a reason to reject its conclusion.

title: The syllogism and the Venn test
description: Aristotle's syllogism: two premises and a conclusion built from three terms, the middle term linking the other two. John Venn's overlapping circles test whether the premises guarantee the conclusion.

facts.text: Aristotle's logical works contain the earliest formal study of logic we have, and his theory of the syllogism is his most famous achievement as a logician.
A categorical syllogism has two premises and a conclusion built from exactly three terms: a middle term shared by both premises, and two others that the conclusion joins.
The English logician John Venn introduced his diagrams of overlapping circles in 1880.
To test a syllogism, draw three overlapping circles, shade regions the premises say are empty, and put an X where they say something exists; if the picture then shows the conclusion, it is valid.
If the premises don't settle which of two regions an X belongs in, it goes on the line between them; a conclusion that depends on where it sits is not guaranteed, so the form is invalid.

title: The two valid if-then forms
description: An if-then statement links an antecedent to a consequent. Affirming the 'if' part (modus ponens) and denying the 'then' part (modus tollens) are always valid.

facts.text: In an if-then (conditional) statement, the part after 'if' is the antecedent and the part after 'then' is the consequent; the statement asserts neither part, only a link between them.
A conditional is false in only one case: when its 'if' part is true and its 'then' part is false, such as rain falling while the ground stays dry.
Modus ponens, the 'method of affirming': from 'if P, then Q' and P, infer Q (it is raining, so the ground is wet). Every argument of this form is valid.
Modus tollens, the 'method of denying': from 'if P, then Q' and not Q, infer not P (the ground is not wet, so it is not raining). Every argument of this form is valid.

title: The two invalid if-then forms
description: Affirming the consequent (treating a true 'then' part as proof of the 'if' part) and denying the antecedent (treating a false 'if' part as proof of a false 'then' part) are invalid.

facts.text: Affirming the consequent: 'If she's Brazilian, she speaks Portuguese. She speaks Portuguese. So she's Brazilian.' The form is invalid and often mistaken for modus ponens.
Her speaking Portuguese suggests she might be Brazilian, but it is weak evidence by itself, and as a deductive argument it is invalid.
Denying the antecedent treats a false 'if' part as proof that the 'then' part is false; the form is invalid and often mistaken for modus tollens.
'If you pass all the exams, you pass the class' says nothing about students who don't pass every exam: there may be other ways of passing.

title: Induction
description: Induction reasons from cases to a conclusion that is probable, not certain. Inductive arguments are strong or weak rather than valid or invalid, and new premises can overturn them.

facts.text: An inductive argument's conclusion is meant to follow from its premises with high probability, not certainty: the premises could all be true and the conclusion still false.
forall x: 'Every winter so far, it has snowed in Calgary. So it will snow in Calgary this coming winter.' is inductive and invalid: this winter could still stay dry.
Inductive arguments are judged strong or weak rather than valid or invalid; a strong one's premises make its conclusion likely.

'Tweets is a healthy bird; most healthy birds fly; so Tweets probably flies' is strong, but adding that Tweets is 6 ft tall and runs 30 mph overturns it. A valid deduction can't be overturned that way.

title: The black swan problem
description: For centuries Europeans took 'all swans are white' as settled, until black swans were recorded in Australia in 1697. No pile of confirming cases proves a generalization; one counterexample can disprove it.

facts.text: In the first century CE the Roman satirist Juvenal called a good wife 'a rare bird in the earth, and very like a black swan'; 'black swan' came to mean something that defied belief.
Europeans assumed, based on their observations, that all swans were white.
In 1697 Willem de Vlamingh's Dutch expedition to Western Australia saw black swans and named a river after them; he noted simply, 'They are quite black'.
Verifying that all swans are white would require checking every swan, yet a single black swan can disprove it.

title: Inference to the best explanation
description: Inference to the best explanation, or abduction, concludes that whatever would best explain all the evidence is true. Sherlock Holmes called it deduction, but it can be wrong even when every clue is true.

facts.text: When Sherlock Holmes first meets Dr. Watson in A Study in Scarlet, he says, 'You have been in Afghanistan, I perceive.'
Holmes explains: a medical type with a military air (an army doctor), a dark face but fair wrists (the tropics), a haggard face and a stiff, injured left arm; so, Afghanistan.
Inference to the best explanation, also called abduction, concludes that the hypothesis which would best explain the evidence is true; the conclusion does not follow with certainty.
Finding a plate, crumbs, jam and an empty milk carton on the table one morning, you infer a housemate had a midnight snack; a burglar who stopped for a bite would be a far more contrived explanation.
A good explanation must explain all the observed facts, and explain them better than the competing explanations.
Holmes calls his method 'the science of deduction', but scholars have repeatedly pointed out that most of his inferences are abduction rather than deduction.
Inference to the best explanation is not deductive: its premises can all be true and its conclusion false.

title: Peirce's beans: three kinds of inference
description: In 1878 Charles Sanders Peirce rearranged one syllogism about a bag of white beans to show deduction, induction and hypothesis (abduction), and how much each one promises.

facts.text: In 'Deduction, Induction, and Hypothesis' (1878), Charles Sanders Peirce showed three kinds of inference by rearranging one argument about a bag of white beans.
Peirce imagines a room of bags of beans: one bag holds only white beans, a handful of white beans lies on the table, and he guesses the handful came from that bag.
Peirce's deduction: all beans from this bag are white, these are from it, so these are white. Induction infers the 'all' rule from the other two; hypothesis infers 'from this bag'.
Peirce wrote, 'As a general rule, hypothesis is a weak kind of argument', and he also called hypothesis abduction.

title: What a fallacy is
description: A fallacy is an error in reasoning: an argument that seems better than it really is. It is a flaw in the argument, not proof that its conclusion is false.

facts.text: A fallacy is a kind of error in reasoning. Fallacious reasoning should not be persuasive, but it too often is.
A useful working definition: a fallacy is an argument that seems to be better than it really is.
Bad reasoning can still arrive at the truth: showing that an argument is fallacious does not show that its conclusion is false.

title: Why fallacies convince
description: Aristotle, in the first known systematic study of fallacies, compared bad reasoning to metal that only seems to be silver; fallacies can be psychologically compelling without being rationally compelling.

facts.text: The first known systematic study of fallacies was Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations, which describes thirteen types.

Aristotle opens Sophistical Refutations by comparing reasoning to metals: some things only seem to be silver or gold (things made of tin can look like silver), and some reasoning only seems genuine, since the inexperienced see it only from a distance.
Fallacies can be psychologically compelling without being rationally compelling: what makes something a fallacy is that it fails to be rationally compelling once carefully considered.

title: Ad hominem: attacking the person
description: An ad hominem ('to the person') attacks the arguer instead of the argument. Versions include the abusive and the circumstantial. John Locke named it in 1690.

facts.text: An ad hominem fallacy makes an irrelevant attack on the person arguing and suggests it undermines the argument itself. 'Ad hominem' is Latin for 'to the person'.
IEP example: dismissing a girl's reasoning about Kepler's astronomy because she is only fifteen. Her age is irrelevant; the reasoning stands or falls on the evidence.

The abusive ad hominem says a view should be rejected because its holder has some unfavorable trait; the circumstantial version says it is driven by self-interest. A self-interested claim may still be sound.
John Locke identified ad hominem arguments, with other 'ad' arguments, in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690); he did not call them fallacies, which others did later.

title: When the person does matter
description: Not every personal point is an ad hominem: a witness's honesty matters to their testimony, while an argument can be judged on its own merits. The test is relevance.

facts.text: Questioning a witness's credibility in court is not an ad hominem: testimony depends on whether the witness can be trusted, while an argument can be assessed on its own merits.
The main difficulty in labeling something an ad hominem fallacy is deciding whether the personal attack is relevant or irrelevant.

title: The straw man
description: A straw man replaces someone's real view with a weaker, easier one they would not endorse, knocks that down, and acts as if the real view is refuted.

facts.text: The straw man fallacy attributes to an opponent an easily refuted position they would not endorse, attacks it, and treats their actual position as undermined.
A straw man is a position that looks like the target position but is actually a less plausible one, much easier to refute.
Two things go wrong in a straw man: the opponent does not hold the substituted view, and even if they did, its falsity would not show their real view false.
The natural reply to a straw man is 'Wait! That's not what I said.' If the misrepresentation is on purpose, the straw man is caused by lying.
Smearing the opponent produces an ad hominem fallacy; smearing the opponent's argument produces a straw man.

title: The false dilemma
description: A false dilemma unfairly offers too few options (with two, a false dichotomy or black-or-white fallacy) and demands a choice among them. Escape by naming a missing option.

facts.text: A false dilemma unfairly presents too few choices and implies one must be chosen from that short menu. With only two choices it is also called a false dichotomy or the black-or-white fallacy.
A false dilemma is a fallacy of illegitimate presumption: its flaw lies in a false premise, the claim that the options offered are the only ones.
IEP example: a pollster asks if your employer is drunk on the job once a week, twice a week or more, leaving out 'never'. Demanding another choice is going 'between the horns' of the dilemma.
The key is whether the limited menu is fair: 'Will you contribute $20 or won't you?' is not unfair. Everything is either black or not black, but not everything is black or white.

title: The slippery slope
description: A slippery slope claims a first step will lead, step by step, to a bad end. It is a fallacy only when that outcome is made to seem likelier than the steps allow; some slopes are real.

facts.text: A slippery slope argument claims a first step will probably lead, step by step, to a final bad outcome. It is a fallacy when the likelihood of that outcome is exaggerated.
Arguments of slippery slope form may or may not be fallacious, depending on how likely each step is; the analyst asks how likely the first step is to lead to the last.
Even if each link in a slippery slope is individually probable, it doesn't follow that the whole chain is: the first step can make the last one much less likely than any single link.
When the chain in a slippery slope is about causes, the fallacy is also called the domino fallacy.

title: Circular reasoning and begging the question
description: Circular reasoning starts from what it wants to end with; begging the question is its tightest form. In logic, 'beg the question' means assume the conclusion, not raise a question.

facts.text: Circular reasoning begins with what it is trying to end up with. In begging the question, the premises presuppose the conclusion, so the arguer makes no progress and essentially repeats the point.
A dictionary as a whole is a large circle of words defined by other words, yet it is informative and not fallacious; a small circle of definitions is fallacious.
A premise does not beg the question if the arguer could defend it independently of accepting the conclusion at issue.
'Beg the question' is a 16th-century translator's rendering of Aristotle's petitio principii; a better translation would be 'assume the conclusion'.
In everyday English, 'beg the question' usually means 'raise the question'; Merriam-Webster treats that use as established too.

title: The red herring
description: A red herring is a digression that leads away from the issue, named for strong-smelling smoked fish said to throw hounds off a trail. Its cousin, the irrelevant conclusion, proves a point beside the one at issue.

facts.text: A red herring is a digression that leads the reasoner off the track of relevant information. An intentional false lead in a criminal investigation is another example.
'Red herring' comes from smoked herring, which turns red and smells strong; such fish were said to be dragged across a trail to throw hunting dogs off the scent.
In the related fallacy of irrelevant conclusion, an argument misses the point: the claim that Calgary is Canada's fastest-growing city is not defeated by a sound argument that it is not the biggest.

title: Tu quoque: 'you too'
description: Tu quoque ('you too') rejects advice or an argument because the speaker doesn't follow it. Hypocrisy is a reason for suspicion, not a rebuttal. Its cousin is 'two wrongs don't make a right'.

facts.text: Tu quoque, Latin for 'you too', rejects someone's argument or advice because the arguer does not practice what they preach. It is a kind of ad hominem.
SEP example: rejecting a neighbor's advice to exercise regularly because she does not exercise. The value of advice is not wholly dependent on the integrity of the advisor.
Discovering that a speaker is a hypocrite is a reason to be suspicious of their reasoning, but not a sufficient reason to discount it.
A typical tu quoque charges your accuser with what you've just been accused of, instead of answering the accusation: a way to avoid a tough criticism.
'Two wrongs do not make a right' names the fallacy of defending a wrong action as right because someone else acted wrongly first.

title: The appeal to popularity
description: The appeal to the people (ad populum) and the bandwagon treat what most people believe as proof. Popularity is some evidence, but the fallacy overrates it.

facts.text: The appeal to the people (argumentum ad populum) suggests too strongly that a claim is correct simply because most people believe it, or wrong because they do not. Popular agreement is not a reliable sign of truth.
IEP example: 'You should turn to channel 6. It's the most watched channel this year.' It assumes the most-watched channel is, for that reason alone, the best for you.
The bandwagon fallacy treats a claim as correct because more and more people are coming to believe it. What's missing is knowledge that the thing is popular because of its quality.

What most people believe is, for that reason, somewhat likely to be true; the fallacy lies in overestimating this support. Pointing out that many people studied a claim and reached a reasoned conclusion is not fallacious.

title: Families of fallacies
description: Fallacies can be grouped by how they cheat: dodging the point with an irrelevant reason, distorting it, or assuming it. Logicians still dispute the best classification.

facts.text: Fallacies of relevance rely on an irrelevant reason (the ad hominem is one); fallacies of illegitimate presumption include begging the question and the false dilemma.
Researchers disagree about the best way to classify fallacies; the taxonomy is in dispute.
The core fallacies of logic textbooks spring mainly from two sources: Aristotle's Sophistical Refutations and John Locke's An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690).

title: What makes something evidence
description: Evidence for a claim makes it more likely to be true (smoke for fire); reasons that a belief would benefit you are prudential, not evidence.

facts.text: Evidence for a claim makes the claim more likely to be true, and evidence against makes it less likely; smoke is evidence of fire, not of rain, because it is a reliable sign of fire.
Philosophers distinguish prudential reasons for a belief (holding it would benefit you) from evidence bearing on whether it is true; a belief can be prudent to hold without sufficient evidence.

title: Clifford's shipowner
description: W. K. Clifford's 1877 story of a shipowner who stifled his doubts about an old ship, and his principle that it is wrong to believe anything on insufficient evidence.

facts.text: In his 1877 essay 'The Ethics of Belief', W. K. Clifford told of a shipowner who knew his emigrant ship was old and often needed repairs; since refitting would be costly and slow, he stifled his doubts, sincerely believed her safe, and she went down in mid-ocean.

Clifford altered the story so the ship arrived safely and asked whether that lessened the owner's guilt: 'Not one jot.' He had got his belief by stifling his doubts, not by patient investigation, and had no right to believe on such evidence.
Clifford's principle: 'It is wrong always, everywhere, and for anyone, to believe anything upon insufficient evidence.'

title: The burden of proof
description: Whoever makes a claim must back it up; 'you can't prove I didn't' misplaces the burden. Criminal courts put it on the prosecution; Roman law stated the rule; critics who cry 'fallacy' carry it too.

facts.text: Misplaced burden of proof: trying to get someone else to prove you wrong when it is your responsibility to prove you are right, as in answering doubts about 'I saw a green alien' with 'You can't prove I didn't.'
In U.S. criminal cases the burden of proving the defendant's guilt is on the prosecution, which must establish it beyond a reasonable doubt.
A criminal defendant is presumed innocent until proven guilty; if the prosecution fails to prove guilt, the verdict is not guilty even if the defense offers no evidence of innocence.
The Roman law Digest (22.3.2, from the jurist Paulus) states: 'Ei incumbit probatio qui dicit, non qui negat': proof lies on the one who asserts, not on the one who denies.
A charge of fallacious reasoning needs justifying: whoever claims someone's reasoning is fallacious carries the burden of proof and should be able to give reasons if challenged.

title: The appeal to ignorance
description: Taking a lack of proof as proof of the opposite. Locke named it in 1690. Absence of evidence counts only after a thorough search that would have found the evidence.

facts.text: The appeal to ignorance (argument from ignorance) has two forms: not knowing a statement is true is taken as proof it is false, or not knowing it is false is taken as proof it is true.
John Locke named the argumentum ad ignorantiam in An Essay Concerning Human Understanding (1690), alongside the ad verecundiam and ad hominem.
Arguing from a lack of evidence is proper only if the search was thorough and, if the thing existed, there would be discoverable evidence of it.

title: Anecdotal evidence
description: A firsthand story offered as evidence about what generally happens. One case can't show what usually happens; a healthy smoker fits research reporting a raised risk.

facts.text: Overemphasizing anecdotal evidence means generalizing from a few firsthand stories while discounting evidence gathered by systematic search or testing.

The IEP's example of anecdotal evidence: someone who has read the health warnings and knows the research concludes smoking can't hurt you because a brother who smokes has never been sick a day in his life.
Tobacco use is a leading cause of cancer and of death from cancer; people who use tobacco have an increased risk of cancer.

title: Hasty generalization
description: A conclusion drawn from insufficient or biased evidence: too few cases (one day in Flagstaff) or unusual ones (a first class, the plants on a plate).

facts.text: Purdue OWL defines a hasty generalization as a conclusion based on insufficient or biased evidence, with the example of judging a course boring after only the first day, which is typically full of housekeeping.
The IEP's example: meeting two people in Nicaragua who were nice and concluding all people you meet there will be nice; 'all' implies zero error margin, so it would need sampling every single person.

A good statistical generalization needs an adequate sample size and a non-biased sample; going to Flagstaff, Arizona for one day and concluding it rains there every day because it rained is a hasty generalization.
The IEP's unrepresentative generalization: 'Each plant on my plate is edible, so all plants are edible'; a sample should be like the whole population in the relevant respects.

title: Cherry-picking
description: Showing only the evidence that helps a case (suppressed evidence), deliberately or by oversight, illustrated by a 2007 Colgate poster the UK regulator ruled misleading.

facts.text: Cherry-picking the evidence is another name for suppressed evidence: failing to use relevant, significant information, usually information that counts against one's own conclusion.
If relevant information is inadvertently overlooked rather than deliberately suppressed, the fallacy of suppressed evidence (incomplete evidence) is still said to occur.

In January 2007 the UK Advertising Standards Authority ruled misleading a Colgate poster claiming 'More than 80% of dentists recommend Colgate', based on a survey of dentists, and told Colgate not to repeat it.

The survey behind Colgate's claim let dentists recommend several toothpaste brands, not just one; the ASA found readers would take it to mean 80% chose Colgate over other brands and the rest preferred others.

title: Survivorship bias
description: Paying attention only to what passed a selective filter. Abraham Wald saw that damage on returning bombers marked survivable hits, so armor belonged where survivors showed the least damage.

facts.text: In WWII analysts saw heavy damage on returning planes' wings, tails and fuselages; mathematician Abraham Wald noted only survivors were counted and advised armor where they bore the least damage, as downed planes likely took fatal hits there.
Abraham Wald did war work with the Statistical Research Group at Columbia University, developing a method to estimate aircraft vulnerability.
Wald's memoranda, 'A Method of Estimating Plane Vulnerability Based on Damage of Survivors', were never published externally; the Center for Naval Analyses reprinted them in 1980.

Survivorship bias is a logical error in which attention is paid only to those that have passed through a selective filter; media focus on college dropouts who became wealthy overlooks the great majority of dropouts who do not.

title: Extraordinary claims need extraordinary evidence
description: Belief should be proportioned to the evidence, and the more unusual a reported fact, the stronger the evidence it needs (Hume, Laplace, Truzzi, popularized by Sagan); a higher bar is not a verdict of false.

facts.text: In An Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748) the Scottish philosopher David Hume wrote: 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.'
Hume argued that the more unusual a reported fact, the more the testimony for it is diminished: it becomes 'a contest of two opposite experiences'.

The astronomer Carl Sagan popularized 'Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence'; sociologist Marcello Truzzi had written 'an extraordinary claim requires extraordinary proof', and mathematician Pierre-Simon Laplace had made the same point long before.
Hume wrote that an Indian prince who refused to believe the first reports of the effects of frost reasoned justly: such facts lay outside his experience, so they required very strong testimony.

title: Converging lines of evidence
description: Independent lines of evidence that agree form a cable rather than a chain (Peirce); an idea that fits cases of a different kind gains force (Whewell's consilience). Lines count separately only if each could fail alone.

facts.text: In 1868 the American philosopher Charles Sanders Peirce wrote that reasoning should not form a chain no stronger than its weakest link, but a cable whose fibers may be ever so slender, provided they are numerous and intimately connected.
William Whewell called it a 'consilience' or 'jumping together' of inductions: evidence is far more forceful when a hypothesis explains cases of a different kind from those it was formed from.
Whewell's model case of consilience was Newton's law of gravitation, which brought together the orbits of Jupiter's moons, the planets' orbits and falling bodies under one law.

title: Sagan's baloney detection kit
description: Carl Sagan's 1995 toolkit for skeptical thinking: independent confirmation of the facts, and traps such as appeal to ignorance, small numbers and observational selection, with a warning against misuse.

facts.text: Carl Sagan's 'baloney detection kit' appears in 'The Fine Art of Baloney Detection', chapter 12 of his 1995 book The Demon-Haunted World.
The first tool in Sagan's kit: 'Wherever possible there must be independent confirmation of the "facts."'

Sagan's kit lists fallacies including the appeal to ignorance, statistics of small numbers, suppressed evidence and observational selection, which Francis Bacon called counting the hits and forgetting the misses.
Sagan warned that, like all tools, the baloney detection kit can be misused, applied out of context, or even employed as a rote alternative to thinking.

title: A cause makes a difference
description: Hume's counterfactual line (1748) and Lewis's 1973 theory: a cause is something without which the effect would not have happened.

facts.text: In his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748, Section VII), David Hume defined a cause and added, 'in other words, where, if the first object had not been, the second never had existed.'

In his 1973 paper 'Causation', David Lewis built a counterfactual theory on Hume's idea: a cause makes a difference from what would have happened without it, so had it been absent, its effects would have been absent too.

title: The but-for test
description: Law's version of the difference-making test: but for X, would Y have occurred? Courts add limits because the test alone reaches too far.

facts.text: The but-for test is commonly used in both tort law and criminal law to determine actual causation. It asks: 'but for the existence of X, would Y have occurred?'

Taken alone, the but-for test can reach very far: a person robbed on a detour caused by roadworks could call the mayor who promised the roadworks a but-for cause. For many, that link is too remote to justify liability, so tort law also requires proximate cause.

title: Correlation versus causation
description: A correlation says how two things vary together; causation says one results from the other. Causation brings correlation, but a correlation alone is weak evidence of causation.

facts.text: A correlation describes the size and direction of a relationship between two or more variables; causation means one event is the result of the other. A correlation does not automatically mean one causes the other.
If A causes B, A will be correlated with B, because causation implies correlation. The reverse does not hold: a correlation usually does not provide strong evidence for causation.

title: Messerli's chocolate and Nobel prizes
description: A 2012 NEJM note found that countries eating more chocolate had more Nobel laureates per person, and used it to show that a correlation alone doesn't reveal which way, or whether, cause runs.

facts.text: In a 2012 New England Journal of Medicine note, Franz Messerli found a close correlation between chocolate eaten per person and Nobel laureates per 10 million people across 23 countries; Switzerland topped both.
Messerli wrote that a correlation between X and Y does not prove causation, but indicates that X influences Y, Y influences X, or both are influenced by a common underlying mechanism.

Messerli's note ran in the journal's 'Occasional Notes' section for lighter contributions and was meant as a friendly reminder that over-interpreting correlations leads to wrong claims; journalists took the respected journal as a sign of quality.

Messerli found it difficult to identify a plausible common factor that could drive both chocolate consumption and Nobel laureates over many years, though differences in socioeconomic status, geography and climate might play some role.

Messerli's second hypothesis was reverse causation: enhanced cognitive performance could stimulate chocolate eating, for example if people with superior cognitive function know more about dark chocolate's health benefits; winning a Nobel might also trigger a brief rise.

title: The post hoc fallacy
description: Post hoc, ergo propter hoc: treating 'came first' as 'caused it'. Causes do come before effects, so order is a clue, but the hasty leap from sequence to cause is the error.

facts.text: The post hoc fallacy is noticing that an event of kind A is followed by one of kind B and hastily concluding that A caused B. Its Latin name, post hoc, ergo propter hoc, means 'after this, therefore because of this'. It is a kind of false cause fallacy.

A textbook example of the post hoc fallacy: the sun regularly comes up after the rooster crows, so the rooster causes the sunrise. The fallacy lies in supposing A caused B when the only evidence is that A was followed by B.
Correlations are often good evidence of a causal connection, so the post hoc fallacy occurs only when the leap to the causal conclusion is made hastily.
To be justified in saying that A causes B, A should occur before B, not after: effects never precede their causes.

An example of the post hoc fallacy: a fan notices that every time he buys a good seat his team wins and every time he buys a cheap seat it loses, and concludes the good seat causes the wins. It is an accidental correlation that says nothing about why the team wins.

title: Confounders: the hidden third factor
description: A factor linked to both the supposed cause and the supposed effect can make them move together with no causal link between them, like hot weather behind ice cream and sunscreen sales.

facts.text: The Australian Bureau of Statistics notes that ice cream and sunscreen sales rise and fall together across the year because of the season: hotter weather brings more of both.
Confounding is a distortion of an association between an exposure and an outcome because a factor is independently associated with both the exposure and the outcome.
A runny nose and watery eyes are correlated, but neither causes the other: having a cold causes both. Such an association is called spurious, because a third factor is causing the correlation.
Lightning flashes in Iowa in summer are correlated with Iowa popcorn production, because storms cause both the lightning and the rain that helps the corn grow.

title: Reverse causation
description: Mistaking the direction of cause: the supposed effect is really the cause. Checking which came first can rule a cause out.

facts.text: Reversing causation is drawing an improper conclusion about causation from an assumption that reverses cause and effect. It is a kind of false cause fallacy.

An example of reversing causation: all the officers of one company have big boats, so to become an officer you should get a bigger boat. In fact being an officer brings the high income that buys the boat.

title: Coincidences and truly large numbers
description: With enough people and chances, astonishing coincidences are bound to happen somewhere; some also come from hidden causes and selective memory.

facts.text: In 1989 Persi Diaconis and Frederick Mosteller stated the law of truly large numbers: 'With a large enough sample, any outrageous thing is likely to happen.' When enormous numbers of events and people pile up over time, almost any outrageous event is bound to occur.

A front-page New York Times story called a woman's two New Jersey lottery wins a '1 in 17 trillion' long shot: the chance for one ticket in two draws. She bought many tickets repeatedly; the relevant question is whether anyone among millions of players wins twice.

Diaconis and Mosteller named sources of many coincidences: hidden causes; psychology, including memory, since notable events are recalled and humdrum ones forgotten; counting close or nearly alike events as if identical; and the law of truly large numbers.

title: Most events have several causes
description: An event usually needs several conditions together (Mill's 'sum total of the conditions', the fire triangle); singling out one as 'the cause' depends on our interest, and treating a minor factor as the whole story oversimplifies.

facts.text: The fire triangle represents the three factors necessary for combustion: oxygen, heat and fuel. Remove any one of them and the flames stop, so firefighting tactics and equipment are designed to remove one of the three.

In A System of Logic (1843), John Stuart Mill observed that people commonly single out one antecedent as 'the Cause' and call the others merely conditions, and wrote: 'The cause, then, philosophically speaking, is the sum total of the conditions, positive and negative taken together.'
An event can have more than one cause, called contributing causes or partial causes. Which one we call 'the cause' is affected by what we are interested in.
Oversimplifying covers up relevant complexities; when it falsely implies that a minor causal factor is the major one, the reasoning also commits the false cause fallacy.

title: Necessary versus sufficient conditions
description: A necessary condition must be present for the outcome (no Y without X); a sufficient condition guarantees it (X brings Y). Several conditions can be individually necessary and jointly sufficient.

facts.text: X is a necessary condition for Y when it is impossible to have Y without X: the absence of X guarantees the absence of Y. Having four sides is necessary for being a square, and life requires oxygen.
X is a sufficient condition for Y when the presence of X guarantees the presence of Y. Being a square is sufficient for having four sides.

Requirements and prerequisites are usually necessary conditions: they must be met but do not by themselves guarantee success. Practicing is necessary for becoming a good basketball player, but not sufficient.

Air is necessary for a flame. Peanut butter, jelly, bread and a knife are individually necessary and jointly sufficient for making a PB&J sandwich. Confusing necessary with sufficient conditions is all too common in everyday reasoning.

title: Goodhart's law
description: Once a measure is used as a target, people find ways to move the number without the thing it measured: Goodhart (1975), in Strathern's 1997 wording.

facts.text: In 1975 the British economist Charles Goodhart, writing on monetary policy and monetary growth targets, stated: 'Any observed statistical regularity will tend to collapse once pressure is placed upon it for control purposes.'

Goodhart's law is most often quoted in anthropologist Marilyn Strathern's 1997 wording, from a paper on audit in British universities: 'When a measure becomes a target, it ceases to be a good measure.' What began as a jocular aside became a widely applied idea.

When the number of publications is used to judge scholars, it encourages 'salami slicing' and valuing quantity over quality. Salami slicing means dividing the findings of a single research project into many separate papers.

title: John Snow and the Broad Street pump
description: Snow's 1854 case that cholera spread through water: a cluster of deaths around one pump, a brewery whose workers drank other water and stayed well, and an outbreak already falling when the handle came off.

facts.text: A cholera outbreak began in Soho, London, on 31 August 1854; in 10 days, 500 people died. Doctors then thought disease spread by breathing dirty air, called miasma, but the doctor John Snow suspected infected water.
Using the addresses of the people who had died, Snow plotted the cholera cases on a map; the deaths clustered around a water pump on Broad Street.
Of more than seventy workmen at the brewery on Broad Street, near the pump, none suffered from cholera. The brewery had its own deep well, and the men were allowed malt liquor.

Snow met the parish Board of Guardians on 7 September 1854 and the pump handle was removed the next day. Snow himself wrote that the number of attacks had already diminished before the handle came off.

title: Bacon's votive tablets: noticing hits, ignoring misses
description: Francis Bacon's 1620 story of the temple paintings of shipwreck survivors, and his point that believers note the hits and pass over the misses.

facts.text: In Novum Organum (1620), Francis Bacon retells how a man shown temple paintings from people who escaped shipwreck after making vows asked where the portraits were of those who drowned in spite of their vows.

Bacon wrote that believers in omens and dreams note the events that come true but pass over the failures, though these are much more common, and that the mind, once it adopts a view, draws everything else in to support it.

title: Confirmation bias
description: The tendency to look for, or interpret, information in ways that fit what you already believe, and to neglect evidence against it.

facts.text: Confirmation bias is people's tendency to look for, or interpret, information in ways consistent with their existing beliefs.
Confirmation bias includes looking for evidence in favor of one's view and not looking for disconfirming evidence, or paying it too little attention.

title: Hunting for the 'no'
description: The habit that counters confirmation bias: Bacon's negative instance, and deliberately seeking information that could prove you wrong.

facts.text: Bacon wrote that the mind is more moved by affirmatives than negatives, though in establishing any true axiom the negative instance is the most powerful.
Consciously seeking out information that contradicts your beliefs fosters a more balanced approach; people can generate arguments against their beliefs but are not motivated to.

title: Motivated reasoning
description: Starting from the conclusion you want and building seemingly reasonable justifications for it; subtler than wishful thinking, and it feels objective.

facts.text: Wishful thinking suggests a claim is true, or false, merely because one strongly hopes it is; wishing is not a relevant reason.
In 1990 psychologist Ziva Kunda reviewed evidence that people are more likely to reach conclusions they want, but only as far as they can construct seemingly reasonable justifications for them.
Nicholas Epley and Tom Gilovich (2016) describe how preferences subtly shape how people process evidence and recall memories, leading to biased beliefs that feel objective.

title: "Can I believe it?" versus "Must I believe it?"
description: Tom Gilovich's two questions: a low bar for conclusions we want, a high bar for ones we don't; and Kunda's point that an accuracy goal favors better strategies.

facts.text: Psychologist Tom Gilovich describes two questions: for conclusions we want, we ask 'Can I believe this?'; for ones we don't, 'Must I believe this?', a much higher bar.

Kunda proposed that a motivation to be accurate increases use of the reasoning strategies considered most appropriate, while a motivation to reach a particular conclusion favors those most likely to yield it.

title: The double standard and special pleading
description: Judging two cases that deserve the same standard by different ones, including exempting the case that interests you from a principle you apply elsewhere.

facts.text: When two things or people should be judged by the same standard and you use different standards for them, your reasoning uses a double standard.
Special pleading applies a general principle to many situations but not to a special situation that interests the arguer, even though the principle properly applies there too.

title: The switch-sides test
description: Asking whether you would accept the same argument or evidence if it backed the opposite conclusion; considering the opposite reduced bias more than trying to be fair.

facts.text: In 1984 Charles Lord, Mark Lepper and Elizabeth Preston found that getting people to consider the opposite reduced bias in their judgments more than telling them to be as fair and unbiased as possible.
Lord, Lepper and Preston traced several biases to a failure, first noted by Francis Bacon, to consider possibilities at odds with what one believes at the moment.

title: The appeal to nature
description: Arguing that something is good because it is natural, or bad because it is unnatural; 'natural' is vague and often a loaded word.

facts.text: The appeal to nature runs: N is natural, so N is good or right; or U is unnatural, so U is bad or wrong.
The word 'natural' is vague and ambiguous, and it often works as a loaded word that hides an evaluation rather than describing anything.

title: Natural doesn't mean safe
description: Poisons like the death cap are natural, and natural supplements such as kava and St. John's wort carry real risks: naturalness is not a safety rating.

facts.text: Poisonous plants and animals are as natural as any other living things, yet nobody recommends eating them.
The death cap mushroom is the deadliest mushroom known to humans and is responsible for the majority of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide.
'Natural' does not always mean 'safe': kava is a member of the pepper family, but kava supplements can cause liver disease, and St. John's wort makes many medications less effective.

title: The perfect-solution fallacy
description: Rejecting a proposal solely because it does not solve the whole problem, where perfection isn't required; also called the nirvana fallacy.

facts.text: Rejecting a proposal solely because it doesn't solve the problem perfectly, in cases where perfection isn't really required, is the perfectionist fallacy.
The perfect solution fallacy, also called the nirvana fallacy, assumes that if an action is not a perfect solution to a problem, it is not worth taking.

title: Compared with what?
description: Harold Demsetz's point that real options should be compared with real alternatives, not with an ideal; seat belts, which cut deaths by about half, are the test case.

facts.text: Seat belts reduce serious crash-related injuries and deaths by about half.

In 1969 economist Harold Demsetz criticized the 'nirvana' viewpoint, which finds gaps between the ideal and the real and concludes the real is inefficient, and urged comparing real alternatives; economists now call it the Nirvana fallacy.

title: Confidence isn't evidence
description: Confident people persuade because confidence often goes with knowledge, but confidence can be sent without knowledge, and confident errors cost credibility.

facts.text: According to the confidence heuristic, people are confident when they know they are right, and their confidence makes them persuasive.

In a 2007 study, Elizabeth Tenney and colleagues found that confident witnesses are judged more credible than unconfident ones, but errors damage confident witnesses' credibility more; after an error, a less confident witness may seem more credible.

title: Style over substance
description: Taking the style of a presentation (confidence, polish, a smile) as adding to an argument's strength.

facts.text: The style with which an argument is presented is sometimes taken as adding to its strength; a salesperson's smile and good clothes add nothing to the quality of the argument.

title: The Texas sharpshooter fallacy
description: Drawing the target after the shots: overemphasizing chance results or using coincidence selectively, like a psychic counting her one hit.

facts.text: The sharpshooter's fallacy is named for someone who shoots at the side of a barn, then draws a target around the bullet holes; it comes from overemphasizing random results or making selective use of coincidence.
In the IEP's example, Psychic Sarah makes 26 predictions; when only one comes true, she claims she can see into the future.

title: Draw the target first
description: Cancer cases can seem to cluster by chance; drawing the area around cases after noticing them creates false links, so investigators set their definitions first.

facts.text: Because cancer is relatively common, cases can appear to cluster even when there is no connection among them; clusters can arise by chance.

CDC guidance warns cluster investigators against the Texas sharpshooter fallacy, in which cases are noticed first and the affected area is then drawn around them, making a link appear; they must first set out their definitions and methods.
A review of US cancer cluster investigations over 20 years found a clear cause in just one case.

title: The bias blind spot
description: People see bias far more readily in others than in themselves, and higher cognitive ability does not shrink the blind spot.

facts.text: In 2002 Emily Pronin, Daniel Lin and Lee Ross reported that people see biases much more in others than in themselves, rating themselves less subject to biases than the 'average American'.
In 2012 Richard West, Russell Meserve and Keith Stanovich found that higher cognitive ability did not reduce the bias blind spot; if anything, a larger blind spot went with higher cognitive ability.

title: Why the blind spot happens
description: We judge our own bias by looking inward, though bias often works outside awareness, and judge others by behavior; and our view feels like plain reality.

facts.text: People judge their own bias mainly by introspection, weighing their thoughts, though bias often operates nonconsciously; they judge others' bias by their behavior.
People tend to believe their perceptions directly reflect reality, so those who see things differently seem to be the biased ones.
In a 2007 study, people stopped denying that they were as prone to bias as others only after learning how much nonconscious processes guide judgment and action.

title: The appeal to tradition
description: Saying a practice must be fine today simply because it was the apparently wise practice in the past; a tradition is some reason, not always enough.

facts.text: Saying or implying that a practice must be OK today simply because it has been the apparently wise practice in the past is the fallacy of traditional wisdom.
A tradition can be some reason for a practice, but not always a good enough one, for example when conditions have changed.

title: Bloodletting: a long tradition, weak evidence
description: Bloodletting was used from antiquity until the 19th century; Pierre Louis's findings from 1828 showed it was less effective than claimed, yet it lingered.

facts.text: Bloodletting, removing blood to treat disease, was practised from antiquity until the 19th century, meant to balance the body's humors.
Physician Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis published findings, first in 1828, that bloodletting was not as effective as its supporters claimed; some textbooks still recommended it as late as 1942.

title: Chesterton's fence
description: Before removing an old rule or practice, find out why it was put there; a tradition may hold a reason nobody remembers.

facts.text: In The Thing (1929), G. K. Chesterton imagined a fence across a road: a reformer who says 'I don't see the use of this; let us clear it away' should first go and find out its use.

title: Feynman: don't fool yourself
description: Richard Feynman's 1974 advice: you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool; report what could prove you wrong.

facts.text: In his 1974 Caltech commencement address, Richard Feynman said the first principle is that you must not fool yourself, and you are the easiest person to fool.

Feynman described scientific integrity as a kind of utter honesty, a leaning over backwards: report everything that might make an experiment invalid, and the facts that disagree with a theory as well as those that agree.

title: Science tests ideas against evidence
description: Science works only with ideas that can be tested against evidence from the natural world, and accepts or rejects them on that evidence rather than on dogma, popularity or tradition.

facts.text: Science works with ideas that can be tested using evidence from the natural world; an idea equally compatible with all possible observations is not testable.
In science, accepting or rejecting an idea depends on the evidence relevant to it, not on dogma, popular opinion or tradition; ideas the evidence does not support are ultimately rejected.

title: Science corrects its own mistakes
description: Science's scrutiny and repeated checks by other scientists uncover errors, so wrong conclusions are corrected as research goes on; Abderhalden's nonexistent protective enzymes are the example.

facts.text: In the early 1900s the influential physiologist Emil Abderhalden claimed humans make protective enzymes that could detect pregnancy; others could not reproduce his results, and the enzymes do not exist.
Science's system of scrutiny and checks by other scientists helps uncover errors, and the ongoing process of science regularly corrects wrong turns.

title: Popper's falsifiability
description: Karl Popper's test for science: a scientific theory must be falsifiable, clashing with some possible observation, as Einstein's risky light-bending prediction did and theories that explain any outcome do not.

facts.text: Karl Popper (1902-1994), an Austrian-British philosopher, took falsifiability as his test of science: a scientific theory must be incompatible with some possible observations.
Popper admired Einstein's relativity for a risky prediction that light bends towards massive bodies, which could have falsified it; Eddington's 1919 observations bore it out.
Popper held that evidence for a theory should count only if it comes from a genuinely risky prediction, one that might have turned out false.
Popper argued that the psychoanalytic theories of his day could accommodate any human behaviour, so no conceivable observation could contradict them; he saw this as a weakness.

title: Hypothesis, prediction, test
description: A hypothesis is a reasoned explanation; testing it means working out what it predicts and comparing that with observation. A failed prediction counts against it; a passed one supports it without final proof (Rutherford's gold foil).

facts.text: Hypotheses are proposed explanations for a fairly narrow set of phenomena, reasoned from background knowledge, observations and logic; they are not guesses.
Scientific testing asks: if the idea is correct, what would we expect to see, and does that match what we actually observe? Ideas are supported by a match and contradicted by a mismatch.

Before 1910 Rutherford, like many scientists, pictured an atom's positive charge and mass spread evenly through it; if so, alpha particles fired through gold foil should pass with only minor scattering.
In Rutherford's lab most alpha particles passed through the gold foil but some bounced back, so he concluded the spread-out model was wrong and the atom has a dense nucleus.
Science neither proves nor disproves ideas once and for all: it accepts or rejects them on supporting and refuting evidence, and may revise those conclusions.

title: What a scientific theory is
description: In science a theory is a broad explanation backed by many lines of evidence, not a hunch; theories do not graduate into laws.

facts.text: In everyday use "theory" means a hunch; in science a theory is a powerful explanation for a broad set of observations, and must be supported by many different lines of evidence.
Atomic theory, gravity and plate tectonics are examples of broad, over-arching scientific theories supported by multiple lines of evidence.
Hypotheses don't become theories, and theories don't become laws, as evidence builds up; they differ in breadth, not in how well supported they are.

title: The ad hoc rescue
description: Saving a claim from contrary evidence with an add-on whose only purpose is to dodge that evidence; unlike Le Verrier's Neptune, which rescued predictions with a new, checkable prediction.

facts.text: A theory can be saved from falsification by adding ad hoc hypotheses that make it fit the facts; Popper called a change merely ad hoc when its only rationale was to evade falsification.
Popper came to accept that adjusting a theory's auxiliary assumptions is an integral, respectable part of scientific practice.
Because Uranus didn't travel exactly as astronomers expected, Le Verrier proposed an unknown planet; Johann Galle found Neptune on his first night of searching in 1846.

title: How smoking was shown to cause lung cancer
description: Without experimenting on people, Doll and Hill and others reasoned from patient comparisons, a study that followed doctors forward, and Hill's viewpoints such as temporality, to conclude that smoking causes lung cancer.

facts.text: Some ideas cannot be tested by experiment because it would be unethical; scientists can still work out what a hypothesis predicts and make observations to test it.

Mid-century studies comparing lung cancer patients with others, including Richard Doll and Austin Bradford Hill's, led to the 1950 conclusion that smoking was "a cause, and an important cause" of lung cancer.
A study of British doctors began in 1951: their smoking habits were recorded, then their causes of death were followed for 50 years.
By 1954, early findings from the British doctors study had confirmed the excess of lung cancer among smokers seen in the earlier studies.

In 1965 Austin Bradford Hill set out nine viewpoints for judging whether an association is causal, including strength, consistency, temporality and dose-response; they were not meant as a rigid checklist.
Temporality, the cause coming before the effect, is perhaps the only one of Hill's viewpoints that epidemiologists universally agree is essential.

title: Peer review
description: Before publication, other scientists in the field check whether a study meets scientific standards; it is a filter, not a guarantee, and can miss errors or even fabricated data.

facts.text: In peer review, a journal's editors send a submitted article to other scientists in the same field, who give feedback and advise whether it is good enough to publish; authors may revise and resubmit.
To be accepted, articles must meet scientific standards such as building on other work in the field, relying on logical reasoning and well-designed studies, and backing up claims with evidence.
Peer-reviewed work is not necessarily correct or conclusive; after publication, science still has to deal with it, by building on it, finding out why it is wrong or trying to replicate it.

Woo Suk Hwang's published claim that his lab had cloned human embryos and collected stem cells was fabricated; scientists scrutinizing his data spotted duplicated graph peaks, and his papers were retracted.

title: How science changed its mind about ulcers
description: Evidence that bacteria cause most stomach ulcers overturned the accepted stress-and-lifestyle view, slowly, through a community process of new evidence (Marshall and Warren).

facts.text: In 1982, when Marshall and Warren discovered Helicobacter pylori, stress and lifestyle were considered the major causes of peptic ulcer disease.

Pathologist Robin Warren saw curved bacteria in stomach biopsies, always near inflammation; Barry Marshall cultured the unknown bacterium, and together they found it in almost all patients with stomach inflammation or ulcers.
In 1984, with his results widely disbelieved, Marshall used himself as the test subject: he infected himself with the bacteria and developed stomach inflammation.
Ulcers healed by cutting stomach acid often came back; patients were cured only when the bacteria were eradicated, and ulcers can now be cured with a short course of antibiotics and acid inhibitors.
Helicobacter pylori is now firmly established as causing more than 90% of duodenal ulcers and up to 80% of gastric ulcers.
Barry Marshall and Robin Warren won the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for discovering H. pylori and its role in gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

Accepted theories can be modified or overturned by new evidence; theory change is a community process that can take years and involve controversy, since scientists don't always recognize good ideas right away.

title: Spotting pseudoscience
description: Pseudoscience is non-science posing as science; spot it by asking whether its claims could fail and whether its promoters accept a failed test or move the goalposts.

facts.text: Many writers describe pseudoscience as non-science posing as science: it is not scientific, and its major proponents try to create the impression that it is.
Proponents of pseudoscience often mimic science with conferences, journals and associations that share its surface features but do not meet its quality standards.
Signs of pseudoscience in one philosopher's list include unwillingness to test, disregard of refuting information, and tests arranged so the theory can only be confirmed, never disconfirmed.

Critics note that many pseudosciences have been tested and failed rather than being untestable; Popper replied that a doctrine loses scientific status when its promoters refuse to accept falsification.
To "move the goalposts" is to change the rules or requirements while someone is trying to do something, making success harder.

title: Semmelweis's childbed fever tests
description: Semmelweis tested rival explanations of childbed fever by their predictions: changing the birth position failed, handwashing succeeded. Modern tests add control groups, random assignment, blinding and replication.

facts.text: In the 1800s Ignaz Semmelweis worked as a doctor on a maternity ward where an unusually high share of new mothers died of childbed fever; he considered many possible explanations.
If giving birth lying on the back caused the fever, having women labor on their sides should lower it; Semmelweis tried this, and the fever did not decrease.
Doctors often performed autopsies just before examining women in labor; when Semmelweis had them wash their hands thoroughly with a strong disinfectant, fever rates plummeted.
In many medical trials people are randomly assigned to a treatment group or a control group, and blinding keeps people from knowing who got which, to reduce bias.
Scientists aim for replicable studies that another researcher could repeat and get the same basic results; a finding that can't be replicated suggests our understanding or methods fall short.

title: Ethos, pathos and logos
description: Aristotle's three means of persuasion: the speaker's character (ethos), the hearer's emotions (pathos) and the argument itself (logos).

facts.text: In his Rhetoric, Aristotle held that persuasion comes through three means: the speaker's character (ethos), the hearer's emotional state (pathos) and the argument itself (logos).
For Aristotle, persuasion by character works when the speech makes the speaker seem credible; good sense, good moral character and goodwill inspire that confidence.
Aristotle held that persuasion by character should be achieved by what the speaker says, not by what people thought of the speaker beforehand.
Aristotle observed that our judgments when pleased and friendly differ from those when pained and hostile: a friendly judge thinks the accused did little wrong, a hostile one the opposite.
Aristotle's third means persuades through proof, or apparent proof, in the words of the speech; it alone has an argument's structure of premises and a conclusion.

title: The appeal to emotion
description: Using emotion in an argument is fine; the fallacy is accepting a claim merely because it stirs feelings, or letting feelings stand in for the key premises.

facts.text: The appeal to emotions is a fallacy when a claim is accepted merely because the appeal stirs feelings such as anger, fear, pity or pride; using emotions in an argument is not wrong in itself.
It is a mistake to use emotions as the key premises of an argument or as tools to downplay relevant information.
It is proper to pity someone's misfortune, but accepting that a student earned an A on a quiz because he broke his wrist in a game is the appeal to pity.

A logic textbook classes the appeal to emotion as a fallacy of distraction: like a lawyer dwelling on a client's suffering instead of proving fault, it diverts attention from whether the premises support the conclusion.

title: Loaded words
description: Emotive word choice (firm or pig-headed, used or pre-owned) carries a value judgment into what looks like plain description.

facts.text: On the BBC radio program the Brains Trust, Bertrand Russell gave the 'conjugation': I am firm. You are obstinate. He is a pig-headed fool. A 1948 New Statesman contest sought more.
Dictionaries define pre-owned as secondhand, or used.
A euphemism is an agreeable or inoffensive word substituted for one that is harsh or unpleasant.
Loaded language is emotive wording that expresses a value judgment; used in what looks like objective description, it can lead listeners to adopt that value with no good reason given.

title: Framing
description: The same information framed as a gain (90 percent survive) or a loss (10 percent die) can change judgments, though both say the same thing.

facts.text: Framing equivalent information as a gain (a 90% survival rate) or a loss (a 10% mortality rate) can change judgments; people judge the gain frame more favorably.
A 90% survival rate and a 10% mortality rate are equivalent descriptions of the same information: one is true exactly when the other is.

title: Weasel words
description: Words like 'up to' and 'helps' that make a claim sound bigger than it is while committing to almost nothing.

facts.text: A logic textbook points to a sale sign with a huge '70% OFF!' and a tiny 'Up to' in front: perhaps one item is 70% off and the rest much less, or nothing.
Merriam-Webster defines a weasel word as one used to evade a direct statement, named for the lore that weasels suck out eggs leaving the shell intact (they can't). First known use: 1900.
In 2012 an FTC study of replacement-window ads promising 'up to 47%' energy savings found many consumers believed they would get the maximum; the FTC says such claims need backing.

title: The loaded question
description: A question that builds in a questionable assumption, so any direct answer admits it; the fix is to reject or split the question.

facts.text: A loaded question has a false or questionable presupposition built in, so any direct answer implies it, as with 'Have you stopped...?' questions.
Some salespeople are taught to ask 'Will that be cash or charge?', which offers two options and presupposes that the buyer has already decided to buy.
A loaded question sneaks a controversial claim into a discussion without asserting it, and a target who won't answer yes or no can be made to look evasive.
The proper response to a loaded question is to reject it rather than answer directly; some parliamentary rules allow 'dividing the question' into simpler parts.

title: Equivocation
description: An argument that quietly switches the meaning of a key word between its premises and its conclusion.

facts.text: Equivocation is illegitimately switching the meaning of a term that occurs twice in reasoning, as in: Brad is a nobody; nobody is perfect; so Brad is perfect.
Some words share a spelling but have unrelated meanings, like 'bat' (the flying mammal or the thing you swing) and 'bank' (a financial institution or a river bank).
'All banks are beside rivers, so my bank is beside a river' fails either way: read as riverside, the conclusion doesn't follow; read as financial, the premise is false.
Most words are ambiguous, but context usually settles the meaning; equivocation becomes a fallacy when the switch makes a bad argument look good.

title: No true Scotsman
description: Rescuing a generalization from a counterexample by redefining the group after the fact, which makes the claim true by definition and empty of information.

facts.text: Antony Flew named the move with a story: a Scot reads of a shocking crime in England and says no Scot would do such a thing, then reads of worse in Aberdeen: 'No true Scotsman would.'
The No True Scotsman fallacy is an ad hoc rescue of a generalization: the reasoner recharacterizes the case solely to escape refutation by a counterexample.
The no-true-Scotsman redefinition gains truth at the cost of informativeness: the claim becomes true by definition and tells you only how the speaker uses the word.
Words like 'true', 'real' or 'genuine' in front of an ordinary noun are warning signs of the no-true-Scotsman move.

title: Persuasion versus manipulation
description: Rational persuasion changes minds with reasons; manipulation works around your judgment by trickery or pressure.

facts.text: The SEP's manipulation entry imagines Irving, whose reasons failed to move Tonya, turning to charm, guilt, nagging or stoked fears; each tactic could reasonably be called manipulation.
Manipulation is typically distinguished from rational persuasion, which gives reasons, and from coercion, which forces; one view places it on a scale of pressure between the two.
Accounts of manipulation treat it as bypassing reason, as trickery (misleading beliefs or associations), or as pressure, like guilt trips and nagging that make refusal costly.
Philosophers find it implausible that every appeal to emotion is manipulative.

title: Rhetoric as a double-edged tool
description: Rhetoric is any communication meant to change how others see things; its techniques serve good and bad cases alike, so judge the reasons left underneath.

facts.text: Purdue's writing lab defines rhetoric, in brief, as any communication used to modify the perspectives of others, noting that many people wrongly take it to mean trickery.
