Rhetoric can be misused, but so can most good things; the same persuasive skill can serve a better or a worse cause.

title: Appeals to authority: when they work and when they fail
description: Relying on experts is usually good reasoning; an appeal to authority fails when the person is not an authority on this subject, can't be trusted, is misquoted, or when the real authorities disagree.

facts.text: Most appeals to authority are not fallacious: much of our knowledge properly comes from listening to authorities.

An appeal to authority is fallacious when the person isn't an authority on this subject, can't be trusted, is misquoted, or authorities disagree (bar the occasional lone wolf). A film star selling watches knows acting, not watches.

title: Linus Pauling and vitamin C
description: Linus Pauling, the only person with two unshared Nobel Prizes, championed vitamin C against colds; the medical establishment didn't accept it, and trials found it doesn't cut how often ordinary people catch colds.

facts.text: Linus Pauling, an American chemist, is the only person to have won two unshared Nobel Prizes: Chemistry in 1954, for research on the chemical bond, and Peace in 1962.
In the 1970s Linus Pauling concluded that vitamin C would prevent and alleviate the common cold, and vitamin C became widely used against colds.
Pauling was a theoretical physical chemist, and his vitamin C views were not widely accepted by the medical establishment.
A 2013 Cochrane review of placebo-controlled trials found that regular vitamin C had no effect on how often colds strike the ordinary population, though it modestly shortened colds.

title: Conflicts of interest and disclosure
description: A conflict of interest exists when a secondary interest, like money, may influence judgment about a primary one, like valid research. It is a risk to disclose and weigh, not a verdict.

facts.text: The ICMJE says the potential for a conflict of interest exists when professional judgment about a primary interest, such as the validity of research, may be influenced by a secondary interest, such as financial gain.
Financial relationships are the most easily identified conflicts of interest, but personal rivalries, academic competition and intellectual beliefs can also count.
A relationship does not always mean a problematic influence on a paper, but readers must be able to make their own judgments about it, and that requires transparent disclosure.

title: Dismissing a claim because of who benefits
description: Pointing to an arguer's vested interest does not by itself undermine their reasoning; it is a reason to look harder at the evidence.

facts.text: Treating an arguer's vested interest in their conclusion as if it undermined the argument is a circumstantial ad hominem: reasoning should stand or fall on the evidence, not on facts about the arguer.

title: Primary and secondary sources
description: A primary source reports an event firsthand; a secondary source conveys others' accounts and interprets them, at least one step removed.

facts.text: The primary/secondary distinction shows how far an author is from the event: a primary source reports firsthand (or is the first record right after), such as a diary, letter or photograph; a secondary source conveys others' experiences, secondhand.

title: How "let them eat cake" drifted to Marie Antoinette
description: The line appears first in Rousseau's Confessions, from an unnamed 'great princess' and about brioche; it was tied to Marie Antoinette only in 1843.

facts.text: Marie Antoinette probably never said "Let them eat cake".

The line's earliest known version is in Rousseau's Confessions, written in the 1760s, where an unnamed 'great princess' says the peasants should eat brioche; Marie Antoinette was then a child, so unlikely to be the princess meant.

The earliest known source linking the line to Marie Antoinette appeared in 1843 in the journal Les Guepes, more than 50 years after the French Revolution; brioche is a rich bread made with eggs and butter.

title: Scientific consensus and the lone dissenter
description: A consensus is the view that survives many scientists checking each other's work and balancing each other's biases, so it usually outweighs one contrarian; presenting both as equal is false balance.

facts.text: Scientists check each other's work by reviewing it and trying to replicate it, which helps catch flawed reasoning; because the community is diverse, individual biases tend to balance out.
False balance is presenting different scientific viewpoints as having equal weight when the evidence strongly favors one side.

title: Wegener, continental drift and a changing consensus
description: Wegener proposed continental drift in 1912 and was rejected mainly because he couldn't explain the force; ocean-floor evidence from the 1950s led to plate tectonics.

facts.text: In 1912 the German meteorologist Alfred Wegener proposed continental drift; it was not well received, since scientists then firmly believed continents and oceans were permanent features.

Wegener pointed to the fit of South America and Africa and matching fossils on both coasts, but couldn't say what force could move continents; Harold Jeffreys argued correctly that solid rock couldn't plow through the ocean floor.
Wegener died in 1930 on a Greenland expedition; from the 1950s, new evidence from the ocean floor revived his ideas and led to the theory of plate tectonics, now widely accepted.

title: Occam's razor
description: Other things equal, prefer the explanation that posits fewer entities; a tiebreaker between explanations that fit the facts equally well, not proof. The famous slogan isn't Ockham's own wording.

facts.text: Occam's razor: other things equal, explanations that posit fewer entities, or fewer kinds of entities, are to be preferred.
Aristotle wrote that, other things equal, a demonstration derived from fewer postulates or hypotheses is superior.

The razor is named for the 14th-century philosopher William of Ockham, but the slogan "entities must not be multiplied beyond necessity" is nowhere in his texts; his own wording is "plurality should not be posited without necessity".
Occam's razor should be invoked only when hypotheses explain the same facts equally well, and the biologist Kent Holsinger notes such ties are comparatively rare.

title: Weighing a conspiracy claim
description: Real conspiracies happen (Watergate). Judge a conspiracy claim by its scale, since secrets leak as more people and years are involved, and by whether it is tested or protected from evidence.

facts.text: Watergate is the standard example of a conspiracy theory that uncovered an actual conspiracy.
The more people supposedly involved in a conspiracy and the longer it must last, the less likely it is; 'A and B are involved' can't be more likely than 'A is involved'.
In 2016 David Robert Grimes built a mathematical model of secret-keeping which suggested that very large conspiracies quickly become untenable and prone to failure.

Steve Clarke contrasts Watergate, whose theory led journalists to successful predictions about those involved, with theories that make no confirmed predictions and keep modifying their assumptions to protect themselves from contrary evidence.

Because conspiracies hide evidence, its absence counts for little; but Brian Keeley argues that if diligent searches fail where similar searches in similar cases succeeded, we may lower our trust in the theory.

title: How findings grow from study to headline
description: Health news exaggeration is strongly tied to exaggeration already in university press releases: stronger advice, causal claims from correlations, and human claims from animal studies.

facts.text: In 2014 Petroc Sumner's team found that exaggeration in health news was strongly associated with exaggeration in academic press releases; most of it was already in the releases.

Sumner's team tracked exaggerated advice, causal claims from correlational research, and inference to humans from animal research; when releases exaggerated, news usually did (58 to 86 percent), and much less often otherwise (10 to 18 percent).

title: "In mice": animal results in human headlines
description: Headlines often drop that a finding came from mice; results in mice often don't carry over to people.

facts.text: In 2019 the researcher James Heathers started the Twitter account @justsaysinmice, which reposted overstated health headlines with the words "IN MICE"; he said it had a serious point but was supposed to be funny.
A 2021 study in PLOS Biology found that when authors omit the species from a paper's title, news writers tend to follow suit.
Studies in mice are an important step in research, but their results often cannot be translated into similar results in humans.

title: Epistemic bubbles and copied agreement
description: In an epistemic bubble, other voices are left out; agreement then looks more common than it is, and copies of one view inflate confidence without adding evidence.

facts.text: C. Thi Nguyen borrows Wittgenstein's picture: treating each copy in a stack of identical newspapers as another reason for confidence is a mistake.
An epistemic bubble is a social structure in which other relevant voices have been left out, perhaps accidentally; its members lack exposure to relevant information and arguments.
Inside a bubble, members meet exaggerated agreement, which tempts them to inflate their confidence; agreement from a group chosen for agreeing shouldn't raise it.

title: Echo chambers
description: In an echo chamber, outside voices are actively excluded and discredited, so members distrust every outside source; exposure pops a bubble but can strengthen a chamber.

facts.text: An echo chamber is a social structure from which other relevant voices have been actively excluded and discredited; its members are brought to distrust all outside sources.
Epistemic bubbles are easily popped by exposing members to what they missed; in an echo chamber, exposure to contrary views can instead increase members' confidence in insiders.

title: Lunch Atop a Skyscraper: a genuine photo of a staged moment
description: The 1932 photo of 11 ironworkers lunching on a beam 850 feet up is genuine, not a darkroom trick, but it was a publicity stunt.

facts.text: On September 20, 1932, 11 ironworkers building the RCA Building at Rockefeller Center ate lunch on a steel beam 850 feet above the street for a famous photo.
The lunch photo was a publicity stunt: the men humored a photographer drumming up excitement about the building's near completion, and some tossed a football or pretended to nap.
Filmmakers who traced the original glass plate negative confirmed the lunch photo is real, not a darkroom trick.

title: False context: a real image, a false story
description: False context is genuine content shared with false information about it; the image is real, the claim riding on it isn't. Check where and when it first appeared.

facts.text: Claire Wardle calls it false context when genuine content is shared with false contextual information.
Wardle notes that instead of wholly fabricated stories, influence agents often reframe genuine content, so context rather than content is weaponized.

title: The Cottingley fairy photographs
description: In 1917 two cousins photographed 'fairies'; Arthur Conan Doyle endorsed them in 1920; experts judged only the negatives; in 1983 the fairies were confessed to be drawn figures on hatpins.

facts.text: In July 1917 Elsie Wright photographed her cousin Frances Griffiths with dancing fairies by Cottingley Beck in West Yorkshire.
Arthur Conan Doyle, creator of Sherlock Holmes and long interested in spiritualism, endorsed the fairy photographs as genuine in the 1920 Christmas issue of The Strand Magazine.

Photography expert Harold Snelling called the negatives entirely genuine, with no trace of card or paper models; two Kodak experts found no flaw but refused to testify they were genuine. Doyle printed both in his 1922 book.
In 1983 Elsie confessed: the fairies were drawings copied from Princess Mary's Gift Book, with wings added, held upright with hatpins.

title: Outcome bias: judging a decision by its ending
description: The same decision gets rated better when it turns out well; the fair test judges it on what was known when it was made.

facts.text: Outcome bias, described by the researchers Baron and Hershey in 1988: the same decision is evaluated more favorably when it turned out well than when it turned out badly, even by people who say outcomes should not count.
A decision is fairly judged on the information available to the decision-maker at the time; outcomes may have little to do with the quality of the decision.

title: Hume's June and December
description: David Hume (1748): expecting better weather in June than December is just reasoning, yet it can end mistaken, with no cause to blame experience.

facts.text: In his Enquiry Concerning Human Understanding (1748), David Hume wrote that someone expecting better weather in a week of June than one of December reasons justly, yet may turn out mistaken, and has no cause to complain of experience, which warned of the uncertainty.

title: Sunk costs: spent is spent
description: A sunk cost has already happened and cannot be avoided, so it does not differ between the options and should not decide what you do next.

facts.text: A sunk cost is one that cannot be avoided because it has already occurred; it will not change whichever alternative is chosen, so it has no bearing on the decision.
OpenStax's example: $1,600 spent on car repairs last year is a sunk cost and should not factor into deciding whether to repair the car again or trade it in.

title: Why sunk costs pull so hard
description: People tend to keep going once money, effort or time is invested; part of the pull is that letting go means admitting a decision went wrong.

facts.text: The sunk cost effect is a greater tendency to continue an endeavor once an investment of money, effort or time has been made.
Sunk costs are hard to ignore partly because letting them go forces decision-makers to admit they made a bad decision.

title: Second-order thinking: the seen and the unseen
description: Bastiat (1850): an act has a series of effects, only the first seen; second-order thinking asks 'and then what?' to foresee the rest.

facts.text: In 1850 the French economist Frédéric Bastiat wrote that an act has a series of effects: only the first is immediate and seen; the rest come later, unseen, and we are fortunate if we foresee them. The good economist weighs those too.

Bastiat added that the same holds for health and habits: often the sweeter the first fruit of a habit, the more bitter its later fruits. The lesson has two teachers: experience, which teaches brutally (being burned teaches that fire burns), and foresight, the gentler one.
Second-order thinking looks past the immediate result of a decision to its later consequences, by asking 'And then what?'

title: Merton's 'imperious immediacy of interest'
description: Merton (1936): a strong concern with an action's foreseen immediate result can crowd out any thought of its further consequences.

facts.text: In 1936 the sociologist Robert K. Merton listed causes of unanticipated consequences of action, including the 'imperious immediacy of interest': a concern with the foreseen immediate consequences that excludes considering further consequences of the same act.

title: The pre-mortem
description: Gary Klein's method: before a project starts, assume it has already failed and have everyone write down why, to find weak points while they can be fixed.

facts.text: Gary Klein described the premortem in Harvard Business Review in 2007: the hypothetical opposite of a postmortem, held at the start of a project so it can be improved rather than autopsied. The team assumes the project has failed and asks what did go wrong.

In a premortem the leader announces the project has failed spectacularly; each person writes down every reason, especially ones they wouldn't usually mention; reasons are read out one at a time; the plan is strengthened. It makes it safe for dissenters to speak up.

In one premortem on software for military air-campaign planners, a previously silent team member said an algorithm wouldn't fit easily on the field laptops and would take hours to run; the developers had a shortcut they had been reluctant to mention, and the project succeeded.

title: Calibration: confidence that matches your record
description: Being calibrated means your confidence in predictions matches how often they come true; you can be off by being too sure, too unsure, too extreme or too timid.

facts.text: Calibration is whether the probabilities or confidence people attach to outcomes match how often those outcomes actually occur.
Miscalibration takes several forms: judgments consistently too high or too low, or too extreme or too conservative; overconfidence is the best-known form.

title: Keeping score: the forecasting tournament
description: IARPA's 2011 public forecasting tournament scored teams on accuracy; the Good Judgment team led by Tetlock and Mellers outlasted the rest.

facts.text: In 2011 IARPA, the US intelligence community's research agency, launched a public forecasting tournament: about 500 questions over four years, teams eliminated for missing accuracy benchmarks. After two years Good Judgment remained, led by Philip Tetlock and Barbara Mellers at Penn's Wharton School.

title: Proportion your belief to the evidence
description: Hume (1748): belief comes in degrees, and a wise person proportions it to the evidence, leaning with doubt toward the better-supported side.

facts.text: Hume wrote in his Enquiry (1748) that in reasoning about matters of fact there are all imaginable degrees of assurance, from the highest certainty to the weakest evidence.

Hume: 'A wise man, therefore, proportions his belief to the evidence.' Where evidence conflicts, he weighs the opposing cases, inclines to the side with more support, and holds it with doubt and hesitation.

title: Open-mindedness and suspending judgment
description: Critical thinkers are willing to re-examine answers they already accept, suspend judgment when evidence is insufficient, and adopt a position when it is sufficient.

facts.text: The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy counts open-mindedness among critical thinking dispositions: willingness to examine questions to which one already accepts an answer but which further evidence or reasoning might cause one to answer differently.
Seeking the truth includes suspending judgment when the evidence is insufficient and adopting a position when the evidence supporting it is sufficient.

title: The steel man
description: A steel man is the strongest version of an opposing view, set up to test your own; the word answers 'straw man'.

facts.text: A steelman is a strong or effective opposition to an argument or position, set up to test one's own; the word was coined in the 2010s in answer to 'straw man'.

title: Mill: know the other side at its strongest
description: Mill (1859): whoever knows only their own side knows little of that; you must hear the other side from real believers, in its most persuasive form.

facts.text: In On Liberty (1859), John Stuart Mill wrote: 'He who knows only his own side of the case, knows little of that.' Someone unable to answer, or even state, the other side's reasons has no ground for preferring either opinion. Cicero studied his adversary's case as intensely as his own.

Mill added that hearing the other side from one's own teachers, with their refutations, is not enough: one must hear it from people who actually believe it and defend it in earnest, and know it in its most plausible and persuasive form.

title: The fallacy fallacy
description: A fallacy sinks the argument, not the conclusion: a fallacious argument fails to support its conclusion, which may still be true.

facts.text: A fallacy is a mistake in reasoning. A fallacious argument fails to support its conclusion; finding one does not in itself give a reason to reject the conclusion, since other arguments may support it.
Assuming a conclusion must be false because the argument for it contains a fallacy is itself a fallacy, called the fallacy fallacy or argument from fallacy.
Reasonable people won't want to believe false things for bad reasons, or true things for bad reasons.

title: Yes, you can prove a negative
description: Steven Hales (2005): 'you can't prove a negative' is folk logic; laws of logic are negatives, any claim can be restated as one, and evidence gives certainty about nothing.

facts.text: In 2005 the philosopher Steven Hales called 'you can't prove a negative' a principle of folk logic, not logic. The law of non-contradiction (nothing is both true and false) is itself a negative and can be proved.

Any claim can be expressed as a negative: prove you exist and you have proved you aren't nonexistent. Evidence doesn't give certainty about negative claims, but it doesn't give certainty about positive ones either.

title: Dewey's disordered rooms
description: Dewey (1910): a man finds his rooms in disorder, holds burglary and mischievous children as rival explanations, and tests them before believing.

facts.text: In How We Think (1910), John Dewey describes a man who returns to find his rooms in disorder. He first thinks of burglary, then of his mischievous children; this rival explanation keeps him from accepting the first idea dogmatically, and judgment is held in suspense.

Dewey's man reasons that burglars would take valuables. Some are gone from a box, but he might have moved them himself, so that test isn't decisive; the silver the children wouldn't take is all gone, and windows and doors show tampering, so the burglary idea is confirmed.

title: The critical thinking checklist
description: Critical thinking works as a checklist used in any order: possible explanations, relevant evidence, credibility of sources, and a conclusion the evidence supports, with a check on your own bias.

facts.text: The SEP pictures critical thinking as a checklist used in any order, selectively and more than once: formulating possible solutions, determining relevant evidence, judging the credibility of information from others, and accepting a solution the evidence adequately supports.

People seek or interpret evidence in ways partial to their existing beliefs, often unaware of this confirmation bias; one remedy is to hold off adopting a favored explanation until the evidence rules out the others.
